written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: Thirty years ago, my father gave me a small suitcase like the one in this image, filled with his manuscripts, and asked me to read them. I held that suitcase in my hand for a full week, imagining its contents and wavering between the melancholy solitude it would bring and my desire not to disappoint my father. Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets. When my first novel "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" was published in Turkey, I was twenty-three, and I gave it to my father to read. Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us. Unlike my mother, my father—who was concerned for my welfare but even more for my freedom—did not object to my becoming a novelist. Like all fathers, he wished for his son to have extraordinary success, yet he refrained from making demands, urging me only to be free and happy.I waited, as nervous as my mother was, for my father's reaction after he had finished reading my novel. Finally, when he returned, overcome with excitement, I studied his expression and searched for clues. My father said not a word, but—ignoring my mother and the others—motioned for me to follow him into his study. For a time, we stood across from each other, like two schoolboys who had quarreled, awkwardly unable to speak. Then, embarrassed by his own emotions, he hugged me. When we pulled apart, he looked at me affectionately and said, "You will be a very good writer, bebeğim." He then added, like a true man of his generation, that he expected me to one day win the prize I am receiving today. I recount this here proudly, yet with some embarrassment—and his supposition has come true.My dear father died in December 2002.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: I chose excerpt 1 because I believe it had all three qualities of good writing. I felt that excerpt 2 was harder to follow between the flashback and the current award day. I also felt it was more powerful to have the father's direct words "One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day." instead of the quick memory that excerpt 2 provides.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: While I could understand the general theme of captivity in excerpt 1, excerpt 2 definitely created a more clear image and filled in holes that excerpt 1 left me wondering about. The second excerpt is definitely the better written, more coherent, better flow, and relays the story of the captives better than one.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.

It's much clearer and more engaging and it suggests a unfurling story with phrase 'there was nothing we wouldn't give' promising a developing plot point

We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.

He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 1 was better in terms of writing quality. Excerpt 2 had a sentence structure similar to speaking, which negatively impacted the fluency. While excerpt 1's use of writing additions such as "two plans sharing a large pot" and "serious as death" created a feeling of the scene rather than just a description.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better because it uses a more natural tone, particularly in the characters' dialogue. Some of the sentence structures are a little awkward, but the ideas are coherent so the meaning comes through just fine. Excerpt 2 suffers a bit from lack of context in the beginning. It feels disconnected because it isn't clear until a few lines in what the characters are facing. Additionally, some of the writing doesn't feel natural. For example, "Her large dark eyes are like openings to something." written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: In excerpt 1, I can clearly see that the characters were upset about not receiving the service they required by the waiter in the "restaurant." They compared their food to other guests in the place.  There was coherence and effectiveness in the way the message was delivered.  To me, the words felts genuine and there was fluency/smoothness.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Excerpt one feels like it tells a better story than excerpt two. Excerpt one does a good job of setting the stage up front and providing us with more of the context than the second excerpt does. I feel that excerpt one is more effective and coherent than excerpt two.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.

There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Reason:
Excerpt 1 makes the reader feel that we are in the room at that moment, experiencing things as the writer experiences them. It is not just a recounting of events, without emotion. Excerpt 2 starts with a stark line "My mother died on St. patrick's day." That could be an interesting start, but the following it up is only more emotionless description. Contrasted with excerpt 1, which pulls you in with such descriptions like "My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them." You can really feel like you are in a moment, engaging all the senses, rather than just a description of a major life event told in straight, emotionless prose. 

Excerpt 1 transports you to the precise moment of sitting with a loved one who is dying. It's very difficult to capture the strange and sad experience of this, but excerpt 1 does it by taking you through small moments of that day. The things the narrator sees, feels, and focuses on while all this is happening. Excerpt 2 describes these things without engaging the senses or the emotions, and makes the event less important as it does so.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.

Both excerpts again are effective and coherent - perhaps excerpt two is a more honest account - but excerpt one reads like poetry, like a eulogy, while excerpt two is like a commentary. Neither are objectively wrong, or worse than the other. I think because I lost my dad four years ago and the description of his mother's eyes in excerpt one could be the very same for my dad has absolutely drawn me to this text. Gosh, I miss him. 

Perhaps then, excerpt one could be considered most coherent due to the natural order the author pays respect to his mum and notes the surroundings. It's a more peaceful recounting of her passing: '...There was an alertness in [her eyes] still, but what she was looking at, I could not say...' and the language cannot be describe as anything other than emotive and evocative: '... A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her...' It's clear how much he adored his mum: '...The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room...' and: '...The sky lived inside my mother...' and: '...a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity...' The language choice is beautiful and I appreciate it. 

Excerpt two follows an angry, frustrated, and annoyed narrative. I get the impression he feels this way about his mum, but whether it's directed towards their relationship or resentment for her dying I can't say. The language is much more aggressive in its tone: '... Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent...' It's a more passionate telling of her passing through this anger, showcasing her strength and resolve (or maybe it's stubbornness), while still managing to describe her eyes so epically at the same time. 

The mention of Bruce in excerpt two implies the author won't be alone in their mourning. Whether Bruce is his brother, his mum's partner, or even his own son or partner isn't clear, but it adds to a story-like text. 

Excerpt one is a complete text, a closed and finished beautiful tribute and I can't get past that. That's why I chose it. But excerpt two does make me want to read on, I can't deny that. And the ending: '...Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live...' doesn't feel like an ending at all. Excerpt one reads to me like a heart-breaking loss of a parent. It's devastating, but was either expected through his mum's age or maybe an illness. Excerpt two reads like there's something else to her passing. Was she poorly? Has something been done to her? Will she live? I could read more of excerpt two and feel emotionally ok - I want to know what has and what will happen - but excerpt one needs no more words.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: There was no flow in excerpt 1.  Too many commas and long LONG sentences.  Excerpt 2 is written in the first person which I like, and also serves to bring the reader into the story more effectively. Excerpt 1 was hard to read and definitely did not draw me in as a reader.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Excerpt 2 has better writing quality than Excerpt 1. As I read Excerpt 2, I could actually visualize what was happening in the text . As I read Excerpt 1, I had to reread some parts to get a better understanding of what was being written. Excerpt 2 even included descriptive words.

I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt two was easier to read than excerpt one. The excerpt starts with a clear sentence, although the other starts as if the person is having a conversation with the reader. Similar to previous prompts, it was easier to visualize what written down rather than the other excerpt an example is, " the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream." Overall the excerpt was more organized.

A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: In P2 the reader is given more insight into what is happening at the moment, the thoughts of the narrator and what is happening to them in real time. In P1, there is a lot of time sequence switching that is not as easy to follow in terms of memories in the past vs what the narrator is feeling in the moment.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: This second excerpt does an excellent job of drawing you into the imagery both of the physical world around the writer and the world of their imagination.  I truly could picture Tommy coming towards them, and then the writer acknowledging that it was just a fantasy or dream and coming back to reality.  This makes the piece flow very effectively.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1:
"Well, life's dealt some rather unkind cards. One son, a pukka Englishman—a suit-wearing, diploma-carrying, Tory-voting coward—while my other son has gone from muttering one-liners about infidels to a bloody fundamentalist terrorist. I can't say it surprises me. Yes, I made a devil's pact; yes, yes—but please tell me where was the better option? My father, from whom I could never escape, made quite sure there was only one road to be taken. To hell with it. This is the suffering of the immigrant: of my generation and Archibald's, immigrants by necessity, English by residence but not by birth. For us first-generation folk, those who came here fleeing hardship, there is always the struggle to make a home, a real home, in what remains another's land."

"Oh, that's not true, surely," murmured Irie helplessly.

"It's very much the truth, I'm afraid. The worst of it is, you see, this time spent in the belly of the beast. Two years become four, four becomes eight, then twelve. For so many of us, it is far too late to go back. Better to give up the very idea of belonging. I truly tried to give my children roots and culture and language and traditions, but all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant, the curse of the stuck-in-between. But at the same time, I can't forget what I lost. Balance, my friend. Balance."
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more like a monologue. It's easy to follow and logical. Pargraph 2 isn't easy to follow but it's more sophisicated. Excerpt 1 uses powerful language "all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant." We can understand the main character's mind and his paranoia and self-hatred.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Of course I didn’t think of it as cooking. In my mind it was just boiling spaghetti. I’d pull on my windbreaker and canvas sneakers, hop on my old bike and pedal to the neighborhood specialty store and gather the tools and ingredients I’d need to make spaghetti. A big pot, a thousand-yen strainer, two plates, a kitchen timer, a quart of olive oil, a head of garlic, and two onions. Supermarkets that catered to foreigners sold spaghetti. Displayed on their shelves were about ten brands in packages of every imaginable color. I bought a different brand and a small tin of spices each week. The old wooden creel hung from the handlebar would rattle and groan under the load on the way home. It just so happened that I had an old roasted-coffee mill in the cabinet under the sink that I could adjust to make minced garlic. Then I filled the place with the tantalizing aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, and I’d cook spaghetti sauce by the gallon and bend my head over each day’s spaghetti. Alone, at the kitchen table, no TV, no radio. Spaghetti was the only thing I could think of that was perfect for a meal eaten alone. Each and every time I’d prepare one extra little salad and one extra pot of tea…and each and every time my spaghetti would be submerged, swallowed up. Completely. So it was Spaghetti Days, from Sunday to Sunday.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.

The language is evocative and descriptive. Both are fluent but again excerpt 1 has more flair to it. The ideas flow well but it's more than that, it's actually interesting to read.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. She snipped a length of white thread from the spool in her sewing box, and gently pressed a small pair of scissors into the steaming water. When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt one seemed better written than excerpt two, which did not flow as well. Both created an image of the birth and death of this woman's child but excerpt one did so while also relaying the emotion of that event. Excerpt two felt like it was just a description lacked the strength of that emotion.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. I want to give Robbie and Cecilia what they lost out on in life. They both died because of a simple mistake which, although it grew in significance over the years, was not difficult to expunge. Or rather, I've always known the choice was mine. Was it right, however, to let them forgive? I've no doubt my fellow criminals are either behind bars or in important salaried positions. Hypocrites—I needed their praise and confirmation, and my sisters' doubts and contempt, in order to be cured. But now I must sleep. I will close my eyes and sleep. What purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on June 1, 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station? written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning he sat in a red car moldering in his dead uncle's garage, hidden from view, eating Lorna Doones and listening to traffic reports, justifying to God his intent to liquidate the present, more evil, more avaricious premier. Hadn't he already demonstrated superb moral consistency by personally garroting the former premier in the Department of Rhetoric's parking garage? Hadn't he, that evening, leapt into his own pit of blood and terror, and since paid the price in terms of panic attacks and nightmares, for the advancement of humanity? Would he now declare that brave killing a merely private matter by failing to publicly acknowledge his authorship and radicalize the masses to move on, killing each corrupt premier for years to come until, exhausted, he handed the torch to some fierce young protégé? Would he? Or would he turn coward and slink back to a pasty-gray anonymous existence, wherein he walked around guilty, not of a specific criminal act (for he still held his rationale sound and remembered the strangled look of terror on the premier's face with satisfaction), but of doing nothing overall, nothing yet memorable, in the direction of righteousness? Dear Lord, if at this late date he turned cowardly, wouldn't he hate himself worse than ever? Wouldn't he? And then he leaped out of the car.

The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning he sat in a red car moldering in his dead uncle's garage, hidden from view, eating Lorna Doones and listening to traffic reports, justifying to God his intent to liquidate the present, more evil, more avaricious premier. Hadn't he already demonstrated superb moral consistency by personally garroting the former premier in the Department of Rhetoric's parking garage? Hadn't he, that evening, leapt into his own pit of blood and terror, and since paid the price in terms of panic attacks and nightmares, for the advancement of humanity? Would he now declare that brave killing a merely private matter by failing to publicly acknowledge his authorship and radicalize the masses to move on, killing each corrupt premier for years to come until, exhausted, he handed the torch to some fierce young protégé? Would he? Or would he turn coward and slink back to a pasty-gray anonymous existence, wherein he walked around guilty, not of a specific criminal act (for he still held his rationale sound and remembered the strangled look of terror on the premier's face with satisfaction), but of doing nothing overall, nothing yet memorable, in the direction of righteousness? Dear Lord, if at this late date he turned cowardly, wouldn't he hate himself worse than ever? Wouldn't he? And then he leaped out of the car.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 flows coherently from one thought to the next. It makes you feel as if you are there with him in the garage. The Bang alert in Excerpt interrupts up the the flow of what is occurring between him and his uncles ghost. The main idea of except 1 is scattered while except 2 is more effective in that it doesn't scatter from one thought to another.
