Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 2 is more coherent and gradually builds up a clearer picture of the neighbourhood and the family involved in the incident. It builds a vivid description of Patty that is effective in being able to visualise her and her actions, and develops intrigue for the reader who is wondering what could have happened.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: A billionaire once invited me to lunch at his club in London. It was a grand place, but the billionaire wore skinny jeans, a hooded top, and designer trainers without a care in the world. He was very keen to show me his latest software project, which was a program that could predict which employees in a company would next betray their boss. I had to catch a plane immediately afterwards and so was a little restless, and he insisted on paying for my taxi to the airport, which was nice, since I'd come with a suitcase. We were supposed to be talking about a literary magazine he wanted to start, and I hadn't expected his personal security software to come up. But when we sat down and started, it was he who told me the story of his life. I assembled the biography: a humble beginning, the lessons in work and intellect, and finally this  tawny-haired and surprisingly well-muscled figure at the table across from me. I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money. He told me a lot more – about the complexity and immensity of his entrepreneurial schemes, such as a floating wind farm that would house and provide credit for its workers and thereby solve the problem of world poverty and ecocide; or another scheme he had for legally disposing of lawyers from people's personal lives. He also mentioned that he'd taken up playing drums in a rock band every Thursday night, because why not; and that he was presently expecting his eleventh child, counting the Guatemalan quadruplets he and his wife had adopted earlier. The billionaire talked for so long that I couldn’t keep up with it all, I was almost too exhausted to follow. Waitresses kept arriving, removing dishes and bringing huge plates of lobster and bottles of fine wine. His focus was so scattered, his enthusiasm so limitless, it was almost like that of a child. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, putting me in the taxi afterwards, though I didn't remember mentioning I was going there.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: I was invited to lunch by a billionaire who wanted to start a literary magazine. The London club was opulent, the atmosphere carefully crafted through gilded light fixtures and dark accents. I was late, carrying my heavy suitcase and sweating, but the billionaire wore casual clothes and seemed unbothered by my lateness, launching into an explanation of his software project for predicting employee betrayal. The literary journal had not come up when the waitress brought bread to us, nor when she brought a range of appetizers. I realized the billionaire had ordered for us both. He insisted then on paying for a taxi to the airport, a generosity I would not decline given the rush of my morning. As we ate, he unfurled his life story. ‘It’s all what you’d expect,’ he said. ‘Rags-to-riches, you know—to be rich and unbothered, that’s the real achievement. To feel calm,’ he told me. ‘That’s what it allows.’ I wondered if he thought of the literary magazine as an entry point into writing. Everyone wants to write, I’ve noticed; everyone imagines themselves a writer, even if they have never put pen to paper. The billionaire had funded a good many ambitious ventures. A floating wind farm with worker houses, and something about a scheme to eliminate lawyers for managing personal matters. The waitress brought small plates, caviar and shaved truffle and mint suspended artfully over a scallop. The billionaire played drums in a rock band to relax. He was expecting his eleventh child, a number of children he knew and hoped that I would balk at, and explained that four of his children were adopted Guatemalan quadruplets. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: I do not like the voice of author in excerpt one as right from the start it feels braggadocios without even fully knowing what the point to the story is. Excerpt 2 is much cleaner and laid out in a way that feels interesting and lends itself to my curiosity.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Your fiancé is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn't believe in letting shit slide. She catches you cheating (Well, more like she busts you out. Let’s be honest: You were sloppy.) After you left her your phone, she discovered that this papi chulo of hers is full of shit—you've cheated not with one, not two, but fifty pendejas!! She doesn’t scream, which would have been better; she sits silent through the whole awful exchange. She couldn't even get through all the archived emails, but she tracked the first one back six years.Bad move on your part, because she told you from the beginning that if you ever cheated on her she would chop your little pito off. But you cheated anyway. So she probably should leave you out in the cold. But she holds you down for a few months because the two of you, you know, are survivors. You saw her through her father’s death, the bar exam and she saw you through las plagas. You know the plagas: no job, poisoned liver, too long without a novel, too much time in the night clinic at Holy Name. But fukú doesn’t always strike like thunder. Sometimes it works patiently, drowning a nigger by degrees, like with the Chinese water torture. You travel to the D.R., to Mexico, to New Zealand. On a beach in the latter (the same one from the end of Jane Campion's The Piano that she always wanted to see), she walks out onto the sand and wraps her arms around herself in a way that seems utterly familiar to you, and when you try to hold her she says 'Please don't.' You drive back to the motel instead, and a couple of honeymooners—giddy with how much they are in love—pull up next to you. Their constant smiling makes you feel like screaming. That night, you hear her crying in the bathroom.

This indeed was so easy to attract any reader to get the easy understanding and not feel the words are hard. It was effective by using those few words and i would say it gave some natural and smooth writings

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: "Race doesn't really exist for you because it has never been a barrier. Black folks don't have that choice. Like, growing up in Nigeria, I knew I was black, but I didn't really think about it until I came to America. Then I came here and—God, it hits you immediately. Race becomes everything. You can't say in good faith race doesn't matter when you are dating a white man. The minute you step outside, things are apparent. When somebody walks into a bar that you are sitting in with your white husband, they don't see a man and a woman; they see a white man and a black woman. It doesn't matter what they say. At the grocery store, they'll ask you, separately, if you need help, because, of course, it's such a stretch to imagine that you're together. And you are thinking about that, you are aware of that, but your white partner is not thinking about it in the same way. Or he is not thinking about it at all.So you stifle your feelings because you don't want him to dismiss you by saying you're being paranoid, or remind you that, hey, until the sixties, you all wouldn't even have been able to date, so at least you're doing good. And of course if you say any of this to your nice liberal American friends, they say, 'But we're not like that.' You see, in America's public discourse, 'but' is usually a prelude to rationalization. And when you say, 'but we're not like that' to black people, what you're also saying is that you're refusing to acknowledge the truth of their experience."The host, a Frenchwoman who lived with her American husband, looked amused, as though enjoying the possibility that discord was coming.The poet appeared uncomfortable, eager to suggest a safer topic. "Darling, should I save the onion dip?" she asked the host.The other guests were all watching as though they had never imagined they would feel this way: enjoined in intellectual discomfort by a person they had thought was intellectually like them. Ifemelu was emboldened by the white wine. A part of her wanted to apologize for not playing to the right audience, but a part of her knew she would do it all again.Perhaps she had gone too far, but she was plugged in now, the center of their attention. Even Blaine's expression was unreadable; she could not tell what he was thinking. She took another sip of wine. "So, my ex-boyfriend Curt was the first white man I dated."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. Who among us slaves and freedmen, free-born and fugitives, believes they are due that rare circumstance of happiness? We can escape slavery on paper, but not in real life. The verdict of history is clear: no small paradise like Valentine can smoothly elude it. And America is the grandest delusion of them all, founded on murder, theft, and cruelty. Its architects built castles and keeps while never dealing fairly with Indians or ourselves, venerating a religion which they hollow out with their practiced cruelties.You scratch below the surface and find the blood, everywhere. The white race believes everything belongs to them. The slave state of Georgia is as much theirs as the free state of Massachusetts. They believe they can wage war, put their neighbors in chains, and appropriate the heavens and the earth. One delusion however remains: justice. What to do now? Wait? Welcome everyone who comes to our door or move west to the edge of the continent to escape the shadow of slavery? I have no answers. Who is to say what is right? And when I say 'we,' who am I talking about? In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block. We're not a single people. We're root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities and flourishing. Brick by brick, we built this nation: the roads, the canals, the factories, and even the White House. We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility. We are craftsmen and craftswomen, more than a race of midwives and howling babies, bishops and preachers and dissembling lackeys. No one voice can speak for us all.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: It has a compelling coherence, very fluent, and a good emotional effectiveness. the seamless transition from collective disillusion-"valentine farm is a delusion"- to historical citations-"you scratch below the surface and find blood, everywhere". The language is rhythmic:"root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities" which capture both connection and an aspect of fragmentation. its critique is unshakable-"founded on murder, theft, and cruelty"-and while there is a refusal of easy answers, that ask "who is to say what is right?" The excerpt is resonating with layered truths and urgent poetry that makes it so impactful

But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 2 is the best piece I have read thus far. Great flow from beginning to end, descriptive and evocative yet also simple in it's point. The author's imagery of building America intertwines perfectly with him building up to his conclusion. I was nodding along with every word, even with him justly being antagonistic to my own ethnic group. A near-perfect demostration of all 3 criteria.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.

It's incredibly rousing, it's emotive, and it's disturbing, and it absolutely should be. It should make us all feel uncomfortable and ashamed. It's devastating that our own race (our human race) is treated like this - is, not was - because it still happens. As many people as possible need to read or hear these accounts, and must at the very least try to imagine how it would feel to be treated this way.

Excerpt one is more poetic and layered, but that doesn't mean excerpt two isn't effective. To me, excerpt two was originally written and has now been simplified, but excerpt one has been written to resonate deeply, maybe even elevated from excerpt two. It's as though excerpt two has been finely tuned and become excerpt one.

The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.

The main difference in these two excerpts is that excerpt two is flowing and one can easily follow the storyline. Ideas are well arranged and there is logical flow, unlike in excerpt one, which, although it gives the picture, it lacks coherence.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In the early years of the twentieth century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. The towering cliffs of Yeongdo, an island beside the bustling port city of Busan, overlooked the sea, and its villagers earned a living by fishing or tending small farms. However, Japan's increasing incursions into the nation's politics and economy had raised taxes, and the fisherman and his wife, like their neighbors, were struggling to get by.The couple worked hard, and over the years they had three sons. But, only their eldest son, Hoonie, survived infancy. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, yet he was so stout and strong as a child that his parents couldn't help but sense that the boy was a blessing sent to them. People who didn't know him well assumed he wasn't very bright, so they left him alone, which was what he preferred. What no one noticed right away was that Hoonie had a quick, clever mind and a precocious appetite for learning.In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the fisherman and his wife, who had come from Songdo as orphans, did not concern themselves with politics. When the rent was raised again, the household was forced to give up their bedroom to accommodate more lodgers. They swept their quarters clean, did laundry, and made simple meals for the young men who worked in the docks. The elderly couple partitioned off a small corner of the large front room where lodgers normally slept; and after dinner, they unrolled their bedding behind this makeshift wall, sharing the same room as their guests.Eventually they moved their kitchen—consisting of a brick wood-burning stove and a larder—out to the vegetable garden. In the winter, cold wind sent snow and broken maple leaves through the warm papered rooms of their house. Their humble wooden house, with its two rooms, covered porch, and traditional ondol heated floors, was dwarfed by the landlord's opulent Busan mansion, which boasted twenty rooms, imported screens and furniture, and elegant clay-tiled roofing.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: The second excerpt is clearly better in terms of writing quality. The effectiveness of the excerpt is clear, even when comparing little more than the first sentences of each. Whilst the first excerpt begins by giving detail of "The old fisherman and his wife", the second begins by setting the scene of "the early years of the twentieth century". Likewise, we know that the fisherman and his wife are "aging". In roughly the same amount of time we have learned far more about the protagonists in excerpt 2, making it far more effective and coherent. Excerpt 2 slightly edges in front in terms of fluency too, due to its slight advancement from feeling like spoken word in the first excerpt,  by giving background context and history.

When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In the early years of the twentieth century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. The towering cliffs of Yeongdo, an island beside the bustling port city of Busan, overlooked the sea, and its villagers earned a living by fishing or tending small farms. However, Japan's increasing incursions into the nation's politics and economy had raised taxes, and the fisherman and his wife, like their neighbors, were struggling to get by.The couple worked hard, and over the years they had three sons. But, only their eldest son, Hoonie, survived infancy. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, yet he was so stout and strong as a child that his parents couldn't help but sense that the boy was a blessing sent to them. People who didn't know him well assumed he wasn't very bright, so they left him alone, which was what he preferred. What no one noticed right away was that Hoonie had a quick, clever mind and a precocious appetite for learning.In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the fisherman and his wife, who had come from Songdo as orphans, did not concern themselves with politics. When the rent was raised again, the household was forced to give up their bedroom to accommodate more lodgers. They swept their quarters clean, did laundry, and made simple meals for the young men who worked in the docks. The elderly couple partitioned off a small corner of the large front room where lodgers normally slept; and after dinner, they unrolled their bedding behind this makeshift wall, sharing the same room as their guests.Eventually they moved their kitchen—consisting of a brick wood-burning stove and a larder—out to the vegetable garden. In the winter, cold wind sent snow and broken maple leaves through the warm papered rooms of their house. Their humble wooden house, with its two rooms, covered porch, and traditional ondol heated floors, was dwarfed by the landlord's opulent Busan mansion, which boasted twenty rooms, imported screens and furniture, and elegant clay-tiled roofing.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I think excerpt 2 is more effective and coherent in portraying the setting of the story as well as portraying the hardships of the fisherman's family. Even though I normally prefer more direct wording with less details, I think that since these excerpts in question refer to a setting that would be unknown to most readers, as it takes place more than a century in the past in a non-Western country, I think the more detailed descriptions are better and more effective to understand the story. For example, if someone has no idea about the city of Busan, the very first passage gives enough of an idea in your of what to imagine the setting of the story is like.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
